topic: Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) - Part IV
description: Contained in Part IV of the Indian Constitution from Articles 36 to 51, the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) serve as broad guidelines for the State while framing laws and policies. Their primary objective is to establish social and economic democracy, transforming India into a Welfare State, though they are inherently non-justiciable in a court of law.

sections.title: Basic Concepts and Sources
sections.description: The foundational ideas, objectives, character, and evolutionary sources of the Directive Principles of State Policy.

key_concepts.explanation: DPSP aims to establish a socio-economic structure where the State actively works to ensure social, economic, and political justice, shifting away from the colonial-era concept of a mere 'Police State'.

As declared by Article 37, while these principles are fundamental in the governance of the country, they are not legally enforceable by courts. No citizen can sue the government for its failure to implement them.

DPSP resembles the 'Instrument of Instructions' issued to the Governor-General and Governors under the Government of India Act 1935, acting as operational guidelines for the executive and legislature.

important_facts.fact: The concept of DPSP was borrowed from the Irish Constitution of 1937, which in turn had copied it from the Spanish Constitution.
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described these principles as a 'Novel Feature' of the Indian Constitution.
Granville Austin referred to the Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles together as the 'Conscience of the Constitution'.

sections.title: Classification of Directive Principles
sections.description: Though the Constitution does not formally classify them, the principles are broadly divided into three ideological categories based on their content.

key_concepts.explanation: Reflecting the ideology of socialism, these seek to establish democratic economic justice and eliminate glaring inequalities in income, status, and opportunities (e.g., Articles 38, 39, 39A, 41, 42, 43, 43A, 47).

Based on the program of reconstruction enunciated by Mahatma Gandhi during the national movement, focusing on rural development and decentralized self-governance (e.g., Articles 40, 43, 43B, 46, 47, 48).
Oriented toward the ideology of liberalism, promoting a modern, progressive outlook on national legal frameworks and environmental custody (e.g., Articles 44, 45, 48, 48A, 49, 50, 51).

sections.title: Crucial Articles (36 to 51)
sections.description: Highly high-yielding individual articles frequently targeted in competitive examinations.

polity_articles.provision: Certain principles of policy to be followed by the State.
polity_articles.details: Includes securing adequate means of livelihood, preventing the concentration of wealth, and ensuring equal pay for equal work for both men and women.
Directs the State to endow village units with necessary powers to function as units of self-government. It laid the foundation for the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act.

polity_articles.provision: Uniform Civil Code (UCC) for the citizens.
polity_articles.details: Securing a uniform set of civil laws regarding marriage, divorce, inheritance, and adoption across the country. Currently, Goa is the long-standing example of a state with a common civil code, alongside recent legislation in Uttarakhand.

polity_articles.provision: Provision for early childhood care and education.
polity_articles.details: Mandates providing early childhood care and education for all children until they complete the age of six years.
Mandates taking steps to separate the judiciary from the executive branch in the public services of the State to preserve judicial independence.

polity_articles.provision: Promotion of international peace and security.
polity_articles.details: Instructs the State to foster respect for international law, treaty obligations, and encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration.

sections.title: Amendments and New Additions to Part IV
sections.description: Modifications and additions made to the original constitutional text of DPSPs through successive constitutional amendments.

polity_articles.details: Introduced Article 39(f) (healthy development of children), Article 39A (equal justice and free legal aid), Article 43A (participation of workers in management of industries), and Article 48A (protection of environment, forests, and wildlife).

polity_articles.provision: Added one Directive Principle under Article 38.
polity_articles.details: Requires the State to minimize inequalities in income, and eliminate inequalities in status, facilities, and opportunities among individuals and groups.

polity_articles.provision: Changed the subject matter of Article 45.
polity_articles.details: Made elementary education a Fundamental Right under Article 21A, modifying Article 45 to focus instead on early childhood care below the age of six.
Requires the State to promote voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control, and professional management of co-operative societies.

sections.title: Fundamental Rights (FR) vs. DPSP Conflicts
sections.description: The evolution of legal jurisprudence settling the balance of power between justiciable rights and non-justiciable directives.

key_associations.item: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951)
key_associations.extra_info: Ruled that Fundamental Rights are sacrosanct and superior to DPSP. DPSP must run as a subsidiary to Fundamental Rights.
Stated that Fundamental Rights are given a transcendental position and cannot be diluted or abridged even for the implementation of DPSP.
Sustained the validity of Article 31C(1), affirming that laws meant to fulfill Article 39(b) and 39(c) cannot be declared void for violating Articles 14 and 19.
Established that the Indian Constitution is founded on the bedrock of balance between Part III (Fundamental Rights) and Part IV (DPSP); they are complementary to each other.

important_facts.fact: The current legal position mandates the 'Doctrine of Harmonious Construction' to read Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles in harmony without completely discarding one for the other.
